podcast.body: This song tells the story of Bill Barilko, a defenseman for the Toronto Maple Leafs who scored the winning goal in the 1951 Stanley Cup finals but tragically died in a plane crash shortly thereafter. "Forget that everybody in the band has always played. Forget the hockey pools staged by the band in the crew every season. Forget that they're friends with a bunch of NHLers. And you can even forget the song 50 Mission Cap, which tells the story of Bill Barilco, the doomed defenseman from the 1951 Stanley Cup winning Toronto Maple Leafs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song, the second single from the album, delves into a specific piece of Canadian hockey history. It recounts the story of Bill Barilko, a Toronto Maple Leafs defense player who won four Stanley Cups before disappearing in a float plane crash on August 26, 1951, whose wreckage was found on June 6, 1962. The title refers to a World War II US Army Air Force cloth officer's cap, often reshaped by pilots inserting a stiff object, like a hockey card, after being crushed by headphones. Despite initial concerns about a hockey-themed song's universal appeal, its strong lyrics made it work globally, with Gord Downie reportedly improvising the lyrics while playing a "caveman riff" and holding a hockey card. "But we all knew exactly what he was singing about. We'd been on that trip to the Smithsonian in Washington and seen the 50-mission cap and the whole concept."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
